svg.text: HER POV / VOL. 03
THE PROFILE MAKEOVER
A DIFFERENT WAY TO CONNECT
CHAPTER 03
The Bio That Gives People Something
To Say
The O.P.E.N. bio framework
O — One real detail: an interest or habit you can expand on. P — Personality in action: a specific moment
instead of an adjective. E — Easy invitation: a question or playful option that can start a conversation. N — No
performance: nothing fabricated or designed to pressure someone.
Example: "I make one ambitious dinner every Sunday. The results range from great to smoke alarm. Tell me
which recipe I should attempt next." It offers a habit, a touch of personality and an easy topic. It does not
promise more than the person actually is.
Why clichés stall a conversation
"Love to laugh," "work hard, play hard," "fluent in sarcasm," and "ask me anything" are common because they're
easy to write. They are also hard to respond to. To fix a cliché, translate it into evidence. "Love to travel" could
become "Planning a train trip through New England — any small towns worth a stop?" Only use that if the trip
is real.
Your three authentic ingredients
Write down five things you did in the last month, five topics you enjoy discussing, and three qualities your
friends would recognize. Choose one detail from each group that feels comfortable sharing publicly. That
becomes raw material for a profile that is both honest and specific.
Length, tone and readability
Short is not automatically better, but a paragraph of six different topics can become noise. Use natural
sentences, correct spelling, and a consistent tone. If you're warm in person, be warm in writing. If you're
playful, keep the jokes kind. Avoid sarcasm that relies on strangers understanding your intent without context.
